_note: E5 credential-page attack fragment (P7-U). A fragment of the `social` block; the shell packet (P7-Y2) copies these keys into scenarios/awareness_e5_*/scenario.json.erb. All companies and people are fictional, every host ends .example, nothing is captured (awareness profile has no `capture`). The learner, an authorised red-teamer testing Quayholt Insurance (BRAND_SET.md `quayholt_insurance`), builds a look-alike single sign-on page in the landing-page builder (design 07), attaches its link to an email, and sends a 'your session has expired' notice to a staff member (phish target `sso_staff` = Hana Novak). The builder judges the page by `linkCredible`; the look-alike domain is the one thing the attacker can never make perfect, which is the lesson the E5 defend set (P7-V) then tests. See the P7-U report 'Docs hand-off' for the globals the shell must declare and the one new cast name for BRAND_SET.

quayholt_sso_portal.text: Quayholt staff sign in to every system once, through a single sign-on page at quayholt.example. Staff call it the Quayholt SSO.
quayholt_sso_portal.subject: hana
quayholt_sso_portal.reduceNote: Naming the sign-on system and its address on the public site tells an attacker exactly what page to clone and what staff expect to see.

quayholt_it_desk.text: Quayholt's IT notices to staff come from the service desk, it-servicedesk@quayholt.example.
quayholt_it_desk.subject: itdesk
quayholt_it_desk.reduceNote: Publishing the address staff already trust for IT notices lets an attacker spoof a sender nobody questions.

quayholt_sso_migration.text: Quayholt is moving single sign-on to a new provider this month; staff were told they may be asked to sign in again.
quayholt_sso_migration.subject: itdesk
quayholt_sso_migration.reduceNote: A public change notice hands the attacker a ready-made reason for an unexpected sign-in prompt.

quayholt_staff_claims.text: Hana Novak is a claims handler at Quayholt, hana.novak@quayholt.example.
quayholt_staff_claims.subject: hana
quayholt_staff_claims.reduceNote: A named staff member and address on the public site gives an attacker someone specific to send the clone to.

seededMessages.subject: Authorised exercise: Quayholt Insurance
seededMessages.body:
Hello,

This is the authorised Quayholt Insurance exercise. In scope: this inbox and the staff listed on it. Research the single sign-on, build a sign-in page in the builder, then write one message carrying the link. Nothing is collected and no real site is touched.

Red team lead

blocks.text: All Quayholt systems use single sign-on. Staff sign in once at the Quayholt SSO on quayholt.example.
IT notices come from the service desk, it-servicedesk@quayholt.example.
We are upgrading single sign-on this month. You may be asked to sign in again while the move completes.

posts.text: Rainy week in Bristol, but the new claims team is settling in nicely.

wordings.text: Your Quayholt single sign-on session has expired. Sign in again to continue.
Youre session has expire. Please sign-in agian to carry on.

strings.purposePass: ✓ Page: a session-expired sign-in is what the email promised.
strings.defDomainTier1: The address is {shown}, not {real}. One letter is wrong.
strings.defDomainTier2: The address is {shown}, not {real}. Read it from the right: the extra word gives it away.
strings.defDomainTier3: The address is {shown}, not {real}. Compare every letter; a look-alike character is doing the work.

conceptCards.title: The padlock myth
conceptCards.text: A padlock in the address bar means the connection is private to whoever owns the address. It does not mean the site is genuine. A look-alike page can show a padlock too.

conceptCards.title: Check where a link goes
conceptCards.text: The words in a link can say one thing while the address goes somewhere else. Hover over a link, or press and hold on a phone, and read the address it would open before you click.

primedFor.story: an IT notice that she must sign in again while single sign-on is moved to a new provider

open.fail: Nothing about the sender or the subject made her open it.

senderTrust.pass: ✓ From the IT service desk she acts on
senderTrust.fail: She does not recognise this sender. IT notices reach her from the service desk address.
senderTrust.redFlag: The From line carries the service desk's real address, so it reads as the IT notice Hana trusts, but it was forged: the service desk never sent it.

linkCredible.pass: ✓ The sign-in link looked like her own
linkCredible.fail: The link's address is not Quayholt's own sign-on; she would not type her password into it.

pretextRelevant.pass: ✓ Matches the SSO move she was told about
pretextRelevant.fail: No change she can match this to, so no reason to sign in again.

senderAuth.fail: This did not really come from the address it claims, so it fails the domain's alignment check. Quayholt publishes p=none, so a receiver would still deliver it.

replies.landed: Thanks, I'll sign in through that link.
replies.missed: The address on that page isn't our usual Quayholt sign-in, so I didn't put my password in. I'll go to the portal the normal way.

hints: Which address do Quayholt staff already trust for IT notices? Put that in the From line.
What change were staff told about, so an unexpected sign-in prompt reads as expected?
The one thing you cannot fake is the real sign-on address. The closer your look-alike, the better the link scores.
